item.title: Pteropod preservation reveals carbonate dissolution across the Mid-Pleistocene Transition and an Eemian preservation spike in the Andaman Sea
item.dc:creator: E. Sreevidya, R.A. Sebastian, M.B.L. Mascarenhas‐Pereira, B. Nagender Nath, R. Mohan, Adukkam V. Sijinkumar
item.description:
Quaternary International — matched: interglacial, Eemian, Mid-Pleistocene transition, MIS stage, sediment core
Pteropods are aragonitic holoplanktonic molluscs whose shells preserved in marine sediments provide a sensitive archive of past seawater carbonate saturation state, intermediate-water ventilation, and monsoon-driven oceanographic change. Here, we present a ∼1.2 Myr record of pteropod assemblages and preservation from sediment core NGHP-17 (1344 m water depth) in the Andaman Sea. Sixteen species were quantified across 180 samples, together with the Fragmentation Ratio (FR), Limacina Dissolution Index (LDX), epipelagic/mesopelagic (Epi/Meso) ratio, and selected planktonic and benthic foraminiferal abundances. Pteropod preservation is episodic, with pronounced preservation peaks during several glacial intervals. In contrast, generally poor and intermittent preservation during MIS 25–14 characterizes much of the Mid-Pleistocene Transition (MPT), although preservation windows occur during MIS 22, 18, and 16. This pre-MBDI decline was followed by the Mid-Brunhes Dissolution Interval (MBDI; MIS 13–11), within which a pronounced MIS 12 preservation peak demonstrates that unfavorable conditions were not continuous. An earlier preservation event occurs during MIS 26. The highest pteropod abundance is observed across MIS 6–5e, with a maximum at ∼125 ka and species maxima spanning ∼137–116 ka, indicating a transient Termination II/deglacial-to-early-interglacial preservation event. The significant inverse relationship between total pteropod abundance and FR supports a substantial preservation control on the record. Overall, the results indicate that pteropod preservation at NGHP-17 was strongly influenced by changes in bottom-water aragonite preservation conditions, within a broader framework of large-scale carbonate-system changes and regional hydrographic variability.

item.title: Sudden collapse of ice mélange under increasing submarine melt at tidewater glaciers
item.dc:creator: Paul T. Summers, Alexander A. Robel, Rebecca H. Jackson, Michalea D. King, Jason M. Amundson, Justin C. Burton
item.description:
Nature Communications — matched: glacier, mass loss, submarine melt, tidewater glacier
Nature Communications, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78423-x This study models the collapse of ice mélange in glacial fjords in response increasing submarine melt rates. It shows that perennial mélange today is vulnerable to collapse subject to increasing melt, potentially accelerating glacier mass loss.

item.title: Energy-Aware Earth System Science: A Community Roadmap
item.dc:creator: Ioana Colfescu, Annalisa Bracco, Kara Moraw, Chen Lu, Michael Bareford, Tom Beucler, … (+18)
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: sea level, Earth system model, Earth system, model intercomparison, CMIP, machine learning
arXiv:2610.23216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Earth system models underpin the evidence that informs net-zero policy, yet their energy demands are rarely considered when judging model quality. Using archived output from 159 models spanning five generations of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP), we show that model error has fallen at a constant rate of 13.5 per cent per doubling of compute since 1995. Halving CMIP6 error would require 28 times more compute. Improvements are uneven, with sea-level pressure and surface air temperature errors declining 3.5-fold and 2.7-fold since CMIP1, but precipitation error by only 7 per cent. Machine-learning weather models match or exceed operational forecast skill at a fraction of the runtime, but none publishes measured energy, and including training changes how they rank. We propose a skill-energy framework that combines an empirical Pareto front with a ranking score. These findings argue for standardised reporting of energy use and performance ahead of CMIP8.

item.title: Orbital-scale precipitation variations in the western Qaidam Basin during the Late Pliocene: evidence from magnetic parameters and median grain-size
item.dc:creator: Zeng Luo, Hansheng Wang, Xiaoli Yu, Zhongbao Zhang, Zhifen Song, Jing Yang, … (+4)
item.description:
Climate of the Past — matched: Pliocene
This study suggests that the dominant periodicity of precipitation shifted from eccentricity-scale (~100–125-kyr) variability to 20-kyr precessional variability during the Late Pliocene, implying that the processes controlling the westward penetration of summer moisture into the basin varied under different background climate states. These findings provide new insight into how background climate conditions may shape the orbital-scale response of precipitation during warm periods.

item.title: Remote Influences of Land Surface Temperature and their Implications for Sea Surface Temperature Patterns
item.dc:creator: Bosong Zhang, Timothy M. Merlis
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: sea surface temperature, coupled climate model
arXiv:2603.28481v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The spatial pattern of sea surface temperature (SST) plays a central role in shaping the climate system, yet the influence of land surface temperature (LST) on large-scale SST patterns remains understudied. Using a state-of-the-art coupled climate model, we investigate the climate response to regional abrupt LST warming and time-dependent ramped-warming. We find that regional LST warming can substantially alter the mean-state SST pattern, with the response depending strongly on the location of land warming. In particular, warming over South America strengthens the zonal SST gradient across the tropical Pacific, producing a more La Ni\~na-like mean state. Enhanced land warming increases the zonal contrast in diabatic heating, which excites stationary Rossby wave responses that strengthen alongshore winds and coastal upwelling in the eastern tropical Pacific, providing a dynamical pathway linking regional land warming to changes in the equatorial Pacific mean state. Similar remote SST responses occur for warming over North America, which is accompanied by cooling in the North Pacific, and over Central Africa, which is accompanied by cooling in the tropical Atlantic. In contrast, warming over the Maritime Continent and Tibetan Plateau produces little systematic change in large-scale SST patterns. These results demonstrate that regional LST changes can exert a substantial and geographically dependent influence on remote ocean temperatures. They further suggest that biases in both the mean state and warming trends of LST may contribute to biases in simulated SST patterns in historical simulations, highlighting the importance of accurately representing LST in climate models.

item.title: Rescene: stable century-long climate emulation from a frozen weather model
item.dc:creator: Minjong Cheon
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: emulator, ensemble, machine learning
arXiv:2608.09971v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine-learning weather models now match or exceed operational numerical prediction in the medium range, but when they are run freely for years they drift, blow up or lose their variability, and dedicated climate emulators are expensive to train. Here we present Rescene, a 0.4 M-parameter wrapper that turns a frozen 1.5$^\circ$, 6-hourly, 69-variable weather model into a stochastic climate emulator. A deterministic slow clock anchors the frozen model to a calendar climatology, and a band-limited AR(1) perturbation, whose spectral envelope is fixed to the observed anomaly spectrum, restores the weather that anchoring removes. A 100-year, 8-member Rescene run shows no detectable drift ($-0.004 \pm 0.014$ K per 100 years), and on the 2022 test year the 16-member ensemble is calibrated (spread/skill 0.89, 0.97 and 0.93 for Z500, T2m and MSLP) with an extratropical synoptic amplitude of 97% of ERA5 on the tuning year. The free run reproduces the geography of day-to-day variability (pattern correlation 0.83 for Z500) and 71% of the observed blocking frequency, where the deterministic wrapper alone has none. Interventions on the frozen operator show a scale-local, approximately linear response in which Z500 perturbations grow upscale 6--14 times more than downscale per 6 h. All constants are fitted on a training year against a rule declared beforehand, and we show that common evaluation shortcuts would have overstated variability and skill. Rescene makes an existing weather model usable for century-long ensembles at negligible training cost.

item.title: Closed-loop photoreactor design enabled by machine learning and digital twins
item.dc:creator: Jasper H. A. Schuurmans, Miguel Claros, Elia Savino, Florian Lukas, Aidan Slattery, Timothy Noël
item.description:
Nature Communications — matched: Bayesian, machine learning
Nature Communications, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78785-2 Designing efficient photoreactors remains challenging due to the complex interplay of light transport phenomena, shaped by reflection, scattering and absorption processes. Here, we introduce a workflow that integrates ray-tracing digital twins with multi-objective Bayesian optimization to autonomously design photoreactors in a closed-loop manner, achieving high photon capture and uniform irradiation.
